prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "Mastercard Inc" (ticker MA). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: Mastercard has several Rule Breaker traits: a globally recognised brand, strong management and a network that keeps growing, but it is a mature incumbent in a duopoly rather than the top dog of an emerging industry. Its shares rose only about 8% over the past year (from roughly $560 to $604.80), trailing the market, though they rebounded about 23% from June 2026 lows.
summaries.buffett: Mastercard fits Buffett's tenets closely: a simple toll-road business, net revenue up every year from $15,301M (2020) to $32,791M (2025), returns on equity above 190% and free cash flow above net income. Berkshire Hathaway has long owned it; the gap is price, at about 33 times trailing earnings there is little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Mastercard is the kind of wonderful business Munger favoured: a two-sided network with a 57.6% operating margin (2025) that takes no credit risk. Inverting, the main ways it could fail are regulation (interchange litigation, the Credit Card Competition Act), issuers moving debit to other networks, and account-to-account or stablecoin rails, all real but slow-moving.
summaries.lynch: Mastercard is a stalwart with fast-grower traits: GAAP diluted EPS rose from $3.35 in 2015 to $16.52 in 2025. Lynch's price tests are not met, since a trailing P/E of about 33 is well above its high-teens earnings growth, insiders are net sellers and the stock is widely owned.
summaries.fisher: Mastercard scores well on Fisher's points: a long runway in digital payments, steady new products (tokenization, Agent Pay for AI agents, stablecoin settlement via BVNK, cyber and identity services) and strong selling to banks. The weaker points are that it does not report R&D separately and management is professional rather than founder-led.
summaries.graham: Mastercard fails Graham's defensive price tests: about 43 times three-year average earnings and P/E times P/B above 3,000, versus Graham's 22.5, because buybacks have shrunk book equity to $5,606M. It is large, has been profitable every year for ten years and has paid dividends every year since its 2006 IPO.
summaries.thiel: Mastercard is a near-monopoly network (with Visa) with strong distribution through thousands of banks and durable network effects. It does not answer Thiel's questions about a new 10x technology or a secret others miss, because it is a decades-old incumbent.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable compounders with catalysts at reasonable prices; Mastercard compounds revenue in the low-to-mid teens with exposure to agentic commerce, stablecoins and services. At about 28 times forward earnings after a year of lagging the market, it reads as a quality compounder rather than a high-conviction rerating story.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller focuses on liquidity, earnings momentum and price trends; Mastercard's earnings are steady (Q2 2026 net income up 19%) rather than sharply accelerating, and its share price trailed the market over the past year before a strong rebound since June. It is a defensive compounder rather than a macro-driven, concentrated bet.
summaries.smith: Mastercard is a textbook Terry Smith-style holding: very high returns on capital, operating margins near 60%, cash conversion above 100% and growth from the shift away from cash. The question for Smith would be whether a free-cash-flow yield of about 3.1% is too much to pay.
summaries.greenblatt: Mastercard ranks very high on return on capital but poorly on earnings yield: enterprise value of about $543B against 2025 operating income of $18,897M gives an EBIT yield near 3.5%. That combination would not put it near the top of the Magic Formula screen.
summaries.akre: Mastercard fits all three legs of Akre's stool: an extraordinary business, skilled and shareholder-minded management, and room to reinvest in value-added services (up 18% currency-neutral in Q2 2026). Akre Capital has long held Mastercard as one of its largest positions, though most cash is returned through buybacks rather than reinvested.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai seeks simple businesses bought cheaply during temporary distress with low downside risk; Mastercard is simple and low-risk but neither distressed nor cheap. It would fit his approach only after a sharp, temporary sell-off, for example on a regulatory scare.
summaries.wood: Mastercard is not an ARK-style disruptive innovator; it is more often cast as an incumbent exposed to blockchain, stablecoins and real-time payments. Its purchase of stablecoin firm BVNK (up to $1.8B, 2026) and Agent Pay for AI agents give it some exposure to ARK themes, but it is not a leader in them.
summaries.ackman: Mastercard matches Ackman's criteria for a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative business with a dominant position and high barriers to entry. Pershing Square is not known as a current Mastercard holder, and the price leaves limited upside by his standards.
summaries.sleep: Mastercard has scale economics but keeps most of the benefit as margin rather than sharing it with customers as Nick Sleep's 'scale economics shared' model prefers. Its position in 10-20 years looks durable but not clearly stronger, given regulatory and alternative-rails pressure.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets and products that solve painful problems; Mastercard solves the painful problem of trusted payments across more than 200 countries and territories. As a mature public company it is far from the early-stage, market-creating ventures Sequoia backed.

momentum.evidence: The shares rose only about 8% over the past year (roughly $560 in mid-October 2025 to $604.80 on October 13, 2026), trailing the S&P 500, although they are up about 23% from the June 2026 lows near $490.

g4.evidence: Mastercard is led by CEO Michael Miebach (since 2021) and has long been held by well-known investors such as Berkshire Hathaway and Akre Capital.

g6.evidence: Commentators often call it expensive at about 33 times trailing earnings, though 40 analysts' consensus is still a Strong Buy with a $670 average target.

simple.evidence: Mastercard earns small fees on card payments and related services run over its network and takes no credit risk, a model a generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: Net revenue rose every year from $15,301M in 2020 to $32,791M in 2025 (it dipped only in pandemic-hit 2020), with operating margins above 50% throughout.

integrity.evidence: Mastercard reports clearly, returns most cash through buybacks and dividends (diluted shares down from 1,006M in 2020 to 883M in Q2 2026) and has an independent board, though executive pay is high and insiders sell regularly under 10b5-1 plans.

b6.evidence: Acquisitions such as Recorded Future (2024) and BVNK (up to $1.8B, 2026) are bolt-on technology deals tied to its network and services rather than empire-building.

roic.evidence: 2025 net income of $14,968M was 193% of year-end equity of $7,746M, and total debt of $24,643M is modest against $16,433M of 2025 free cash flow.

fcf.evidence: 2025 free cash flow was $16,433M ($17,648M operating cash flow less $1,215M of capex and capitalized software) against net income of $14,968M, about 110% conversion.

b10.evidence: Mastercard's market value of about $530B is far above the earnings it has retained since its 2006 IPO, as profits compounded while it bought back shares.

safety.evidence: At about 33 times trailing and 28 times forward earnings, the share price is not well below a conservative estimate of value.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 28 is high but arguably reasonable for ~60% operating margins and low-to-mid-teens revenue growth.

mu5.evidence: With no credit risk, a duopoly network and near-universal acceptance, the main failure paths are regulation and a shift to account-to-account or stablecoin rails, both slow.

reinvest.evidence: Mastercard needs little capital, so it returns most profit ($11,727M of buybacks and $2,756M of dividends in 2025); reinvestment in services and new flows earns high returns but is small relative to cash generated.

ly2.evidence: It is a stalwart with fast-grower traits whose story is simple: more of the world's payments move from cash to cards and digital credentials, plus growing services.

ly3.evidence: A trailing P/E of about 33 is well above earnings growth of about 19% (diluted EPS $13.89 in 2024 to $16.52 in 2025).

runway.evidence: Cash and checks still carry trillions of dollars of payments, and Mastercard is expanding in commercial and B2B payments, value-added services, stablecoins and agentic commerce.

ly7.evidence: The company keeps cutting its share count (diluted shares 927M in 2024 to 906M in 2025), but insiders have made no open-market purchases and sold about $50.7M recently, including about $27M by CEO Miebach in July-August 2026.

ly8.evidence: Mastercard is one of the most widely owned and analysed stocks in the S&P 500.

fi2.evidence: It keeps launching new products such as tokenization, Click to Pay, Agent Pay for AI agents, stablecoin settlement and cyber/identity services.

fi3.evidence: Technology investment produced widely adopted standards such as contactless and network tokens, and value-added services revenue grew 23% in 2025.

fi4.evidence: Mastercard wins and renews multi-year issuer and merchant agreements worldwide, with payment network rebates and incentives up 16% in 2025 to win deals.

longterm.evidence: Management invests in long-horizon bets such as agentic commerce, open banking and stablecoin settlement while keeping margins stable.

gr1.evidence: Mastercard has a market value of about $530B and 2025 net revenue of $32,791M.

ni10.evidence: It has reported a GAAP profit in every one of the last ten years, ending with $14,968M of net income in 2025.

gr4.evidence: Mastercard has paid a dividend every year since its 2006 IPO, about 20 years, just meeting Graham's test.

eps10.evidence: GAAP diluted EPS rose from $3.35 in 2015 to $16.52 in 2025, almost five times.

gr6.evidence: The price of $604.80 is about 43 times average GAAP EPS of 2023-2025 ($11.83, $13.89, $16.52).

gr7.evidence: A P/E of about 33 times a P/B of about 95 (equity $5,606M at June 30, 2026) gives over 3,000, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Mastercard's network is excellent but not ten times better than Visa's; its edge is scale and acceptance.

timing.evidence: The continued shift to digital, contactless and e-commerce payments, plus early AI-agent and stablecoin payments, favours Mastercard now.

th3.evidence: It grew from a small 1960s US bank-card association into one of two global networks and keeps extending into new flows and services.

team.evidence: Management under Michael Miebach is capable and experienced, with a smooth CFO handover from Sachin Mehra to Ling Hai in August 2026, but it is not an exceptional founder team.

th5.evidence: Thousands of issuing banks and acquirers distribute Mastercard credentials and acceptance, a channel competitors cannot easily copy.

durable.evidence: The network effect is very durable, but real-time payment systems like UPI and Pix, stablecoins, debit rerouting (e.g. Capital One moving debit to Discover) and regulation could erode share over 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Mastercard's opportunity is well understood and shared with Visa rather than a secret others miss.

trend.evidence: It is a leading beneficiary of the secular shift from cash to digital payments and is positioning for AI-agent commerce.

dr1.evidence: Q2 2026 net revenue grew 14% and net income 19%, beating estimates, and FY2026 revenue consensus of about $37.3B implies ~14% growth, but growth is steady rather than sharply accelerating.

dr2.evidence: Value-added services, cross-border recovery (+12% in Q2 2026) and BVNK should keep compounding, but most of this is already expected.

dr4.evidence: Mastercard benefits from nominal spending growth and takes no credit risk, but a slowdown in consumer or travel spending would hurt volumes and cross-border fees.

dr6.evidence: Upcoming events include Q3 2026 results in late October and progress on agentic commerce and stablecoins, offset by interchange litigation and possible card-routing legislation.

dr7.evidence: Its predictability suits a large position for quality investors, but the valuation limits upside for a concentrated bet.

gm.evidence: Mastercard does not report cost of sales, but its 57.6% operating margin in 2025 (60.2% in Q2 2026) shows very high gross economics and pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: The free-cash-flow yield is about 3.1% ($16,433M 2025 FCF on a ~$530B market value), fair rather than cheap for its quality and growth.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 29 on 2025 operating income, an operating earnings yield of about 3.5%.

pa2.evidence: Mastercard is not in a temporary setback; results are at record levels.

pa4.evidence: With no credit risk, high margins and a dominant network, the chance of permanent capital loss in the business is small, though the valuation could compress.

wo1.evidence: Mastercard is building AI-agent payments (Agent Pay) and stablecoin infrastructure (BVNK), but it is not seen as a leader in AI or blockchain.

wo2.evidence: Its unit costs are already very low; falling costs are not opening up large new demand in the way Wright's Law industries do.

wo3.evidence: It combines payments with some AI, cyber and digital-asset work, but not several innovation platforms in ARK's sense.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable market is large but will not be many times larger within five years.

ac3.evidence: Mastercard takes no credit risk and owns no commodities; its main external exposures are consumer spending, currencies and regulation.

ns1.evidence: It keeps most scale savings as margin (operating margin 57.6% in 2025) rather than cutting prices for merchants.

ns4.evidence: Its network should remain central, but regulation and alternative rails make a clearly stronger position in 10-20 years uncertain.

va2.evidence: Mastercard solves the large problem of paying and being paid safely and instantly across more than 200 countries and territories, handling about $10.6 trillion of gross dollar volume in 2025.
